transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom / recorded
Attendees: Sophie Tan (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Morales (CTO - Helios), Marcus Lee (Platform Eng), Priya Kaur (Security)

Auto-summary (quick): walked through org-key + project-key topology, quota sharding, burst fencing behavior, and Console demo of quota UI. Reviewed security controls (KMS, audit logs, RBAC).

Topics covered: org vs project keys, sharding strategies, burst windows, concurrency quotas, backpressure, sticky routing, Dedicated pool sizing, telemetry + alerts, required audit artifacts.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sophie: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Sophie from Redwood, with Ravi our solutions engineer. uh quick intro from the Helios side?
[00:08] Elena: Elena here, CTO, we've got Marcus on infra and Priya on security. thanks for doing this.
[00:12] Sophie: Great. Goal today is a focused walkthrough on a couple things you asked for — org/project key sharding patterns and burst protection. We'll show Console views, API patterns, and recommendations from Optimize.
[00:22] Ravi: I'll share my screen in a sec, show the Console and then pivot to how the runtime enforces quotas.
[00:28] Marcus: Quick ask up front — we have multi-tenant usage with heavy nightly batches from two research teams, want to avoid noisy neighbor issues. We're leaning toward a Dedicated pool but not sure about the size.
[00:38] Sophie: Perfect, that's exactly the scenario these patterns address. two high throughput tenants + several low throughput dev projects.
[00:44] Ravi: ok sharing screen now, apologies if the resolution is off. so here's the Console, top level org, you can see project keys under the Keys tab. yes this is the org/project key topology.
[00:58] [01:00] Ravi: first pattern we recommend: project-key sharding by tenant weight. each project key maps to a logical quota slice. you can do absolute token quota, QPS, or concurrency limits.
[01:12] Marcus: when you say quota slice, is that enforced only in control plane or within the runtime on the Dedicated GPUs?
[01:18] Ravi: Good question. enforcement happens at multiple layers — policy at control plane and enforcement proxy at the edge/runtime. so even if the control plane is delayed, the runtime will apply backpressure. that proxy is co-located with the serving plane so you get per-key limits near the compute.
[01:33] Priya: how durable are the audit logs? we need retention for 12 months and proof of access for auditors.
[01:38] Sophie: We persist request logs and policy changes in an audit store, and for Private/Dedicated customers we support pushing logs to your S3/GCS with encryption via KMS/HSM. retention policy is configurable — we'll include our standard SOC2 artifacts in the doc bundle.
[01:55] Elena: ok that's helpful. Marcus: can you show the burst protection? that's our main worry. the nightly batch will spike tokens for 10-15 minutes.
[02:03] Ravi: yep. two models: 1) short burst window with leaky-bucket smoothing; 2) reserved burst pools per org that can be charged to specific projects. Let me demonstrate the Console config.
[02:16] [02:20] Ravi: here in Optimize we have a Burst Protection config — window length, max-burst multiplier, and debt forgiveness rules. you can set a per-project burst cap and a global burst pool for emergencies.
[02:31] Marcus: if Team A consumes the global burst pool, how do we prevent Team B from being starved?
[02:37] Ravi: we provide priority classes and fairshare. the allocator enforces minimum guaranteed slices per project, then gives remaining capacity by priority. If you want strict isolation, set hard concurrency or token caps on sensitive projects.
[02:48] Elena: does that add latency? we can't have long tail latencies during spikes.
[02:52] Ravi: the design aims to avoid latency SLO violations — the runtime can route overflow requests to a lower-cost model variant or cold fallback with slightly different accuracy. that is a graceful degradation pattern. also, caching prefixes and KV caching reduce repeated token cost for similar requests.
[03:09] Marcus: KV cache — we've had trouble with cache warmup across shards. how does Redwood handle KV cache locality with sharded keys?
[03:17] Ravi: For Dedicated we support sticky routing so subsequent requests for a given session or key map to the same serving shard, which keeps the KV alive. for Hosted we use global prefix caching and fast replication; it's not perfect but reduces warmup. note sometimes the transcript shows "K-V cash" in older logs, but it's the KV cache.
[03:35] Priya: Security question — key rotation and SSO. we need that project keys can be rotated programmatically and tie to our SSO identities.
[03:43] Sophie: yes. Project keys can be minted via the API with short TTLs, and you can tie provisioning to your IdP via SAML/SCIM. rotation is supported and we log key lifecycle events into audit logs.
[03:53] Elena: show us an example API call flow for minting a short-lived project token.
[03:58] Ravi: sure, quick snippet — POST to /v1/orgs/{org}/tokens with scope=project:read,expires_in=900. the Console can also do this with one click and auto-insert into your CI secrets.
[04:12] [04:20] Ravi: moving on to sharding topologies: option A is simple project-per-tenant mapping where keys are isolated per team. option B is pooled keys with quota tags, which saves key management at cost of more complex allocation.
[04:33] Sophie: A is easiest for strong isolation, B is good if you want flexible over-provisioning and a shared burst pool.
[04:39] Marcus: we'd prefer pooled for devs but locked-down keys for research. can we mix both?
[04:44] Ravi: Yes, hybrid is common — use strict project-keys for sensitive tenants and pooled keys for ephemeral dev workloads, apply rate-limited guardrails on the pooled pool.
[04:52] Priya: what about cost controls? we need token spend visibility by project and alerts when spend hits thresholds.
[04:58] Sophie: Console provides per-key token usage and cost breakdown. you can set quota thresholds that trigger webhooks and PagerDuty alerts. we'll show the dashboard filters in the next slide.
[05:12] [05:20] Ravi: quick demo of telemetry — here's a per-project timeline, latency p50/p95, token consumption, and alerts. you can create policies tied to those metrics: e.g., throttle at 80% burn-rate.
[05:33] Marcus: can we create simulation runs? we want to replay the nightly batch to see effects of different quota configs.
[05:38] Ravi: Yep, Optimize has a simulator — you can upload a trace (or use a sample trace) and run quota policy sims to see impact on latency and drop rates. we'll attach a sample trace for your first run.
[05:51] Elena: good. let's touch on private deployment and on-prem — some of our data can't leave the VPC.
[05:57] Sophie: For Private we ship a control plane that talks over your secure peering; data plane can be entirely in your VPC or on-prem. We integrate with customer KMS for key material. for air-gapped we have an appliance option.
[06:10] Priya: auditability for Private is critical — how granular are the logs, can we get per-request headers, identity tie-in?
[06:18] Ravi: Logs include request timestamp, org/project key, model id, token usage, and standardized reason codes for throttling events. Header-level info can be included by toggling verbose mode — that'll increase log volume but gives full traceability.
[06:30] Marcus: back to runtime behavior — in a shard-hot scenario where one Python batch hogs a GPU, do you evict sessions?
[06:36] Ravi: The runtime uses a combination of preemption and fairness windows. long-running KV-heavy sessions can be moved after a timeout; preemption respects priority classes and config. eviction is last resort; usually we prefer throttling and fallback routing.
[06:48] Elena: what's the recommended Dedicated pool size for two heavy tenants and 10 dev teams? rough numbers.
[06:54] Sophie: based on your notes — if each heavy tenant peaks at ~120 QPS with 2.5s p95 latency per token, we'd recommend starting with a 3-node pool (A100-equivalent) and run a 2-week pilot with real traces, then scale. we'll provide a sizing calc in the follow-up.
[07:09] Marcus: can you show how quotas are applied via API at request time? e.g., header examples, error codes?
[07:15] Ravi: yes, the runtime returns 429 for hard quota exceed, 202/slowdown for deferred processing, and a 503-like fallback when routed to a colder model. headers include x-redwood-quota-remaining and x-redwood-priority to help observability. sometimes the auto-transcript put weird headers like x-redwood-quoata, but that's a transcription issue.
[07:34] [07:40] Priya: are the 429s retryable? we need idempotency guidance for our batch clients.
[07:45] Ravi: yes — we recommend exponential backoff with jitter and to honor the Retry-After header. for streaming calls, partial output behavior is documented; you can choose fail-fast or re-run.
[07:57] Elena: any rate-limiting at the network edge to protect control plane APIs?
[08:02] Sophie: yes, control plane endpoints have separate guardrails; but project org keys are enforced by the serving plane so even if control plane is overloaded, enforcement still happens at the edge.
[08:13] Marcus: what about cross-region failover? our research runs in us-east but disaster recover in eu-west.
[08:20] Ravi: we support regional routing policies; you can set sticky region affinities and fallback policies. Model variants need to be available in both regions for transparent failover. there is also eventual consistency on per-key state — acceptable if you plan for short windows.
[08:36] [08:40] Sophie: quick note on billing segmentation — you can bill per-org/project or roll up to a central invoice. multi-bill-to is supported for enterprise agreements.
[08:51] Priya: about encryption — are tokens stored encrypted at rest?
[08:55] Sophie: yes, all secrets and tokens encrypted using customer-managed keys if you choose, otherwise our KMS. we support HSM modules for FIPS/regulated workloads.
[09:05] Marcus: show the Console flow to create a project key and attach quota policies.
[09:10] [09:20] Ravi: (navigates) New Key -> name it -> attach policy -> policy builder: choose token limit, qps, concurrency, burst window, priority class. you can preview the effect using the simulator toggle.
[09:31] Elena: I see a "sticky routing" checkbox — confirm what that does.
[09:35] Ravi: sticky routing ensures session affinity based on project key + session id. good for KV cache locality. downside is slightly reduced ability to spread load, but improves cache hit.
[09:46] Priya: about the simulator, can it import our real trace safely? we need to scrub PII automatically.
[09:53] Ravi: there's a scrubber step — scrub PII and token fields before upload; we also have an on-prem option to run the simulator in your VPC if you prefer.
[10:05] Marcus: show error scenarios — what does a graceful degradation look like in the logs?
[10:10] Ravi: here's a sample trace: you can see a token spike, allocation hits, then an overflow to fallback model with reason code fallback:burst_protect. the request gets a header x-redwood-fallback=1.
[10:23] [10:30] Marcus: how do we measure noisy neighbor impact — any recommended signals?
[10:33] Ravi: track token burn-rate by key, latency p95 divergence per project, and queue depth at the serving proxy. we provide alert templates.
[10:42] Priya: compliance again — can the audit export include redacted prompt content? we cannot retain full prompts for some datasets.
[10:49] Sophie: yes, we have redaction templates. you can choose to omit prompt text or store only hashed signatures for evaluation. for Private, you can keep raw prompts in your own store.
[10:58] Elena: ok let's talk pilot. we'd like a pilot focused on the two heavy tenants and pooled devs for 2 weeks. what do you need from us?
[11:04] Sophie: traces, expected QPS and token distribution, a list of prioritized tenants, and compliance questions. we'll provision a 3-node Dedicated pool for the pilot and set up org/project keys and the burst pool.
[11:13] Marcus: timeline? we can get traces ready in 48 hours.
[11:16] Sophie: great — we'll aim to spin up pilot environment within 5 business days after we have traces and signed pilot ARO (access request).
[11:24] [11:30] Ravi: last demo bit — alerting and escalation: here's an example policy that posts to Slack and triggers PagerDuty when token burn exceeds threshold for 3 minutes.
[11:38] Priya: do you have SOC2 docs we can share with our audit team?
[11:41] Sophie: yes — I'll send SOC2 Type II, ISO attestation, and the KMS/HSM integration guide.
[11:47] Elena: any surprising limitations we should be aware of?
[11:50] Ravi: edge cases: very high cardinality keys can increase metadata overhead; if you have tens of thousands of ephemeral keys, we recommend pooling dev keys. also, cross-region state is eventually consistent so tight per-key accounting across regions has caveats.
[12:03] Marcus: cost control question — can we set hard spend caps that stop requests rather than just throttle?
[12:08] Sophie: yes, hard budget enforcement is available; you can configure stop gates that respond with a specific error code and outbound webhook.
[12:16] [12:20] Elena: ok let's recap next steps before we wrap.
[12:23] Sophie: recap: 1) Helios to share traces + tenant prioritization; 2) Redwood to provide pilot sizing + pricing + SOC2/security bundle; 3) Ravi will share terraform/Console snippets and a sample trace for simulator; 4) schedule pilot kickoff.
[12:38] Marcus: one more small item — are there exporter hooks for Prometheus from the runtime?
[12:43] Ravi: yes, the runtime exposes metrics and we have an exporter. we'll include the collector config in the runbook.
[12:50] Priya: thanks everyone, this was good.
[12:53] Sophie: thank you, we'll follow up with all the artifacts.
[12:57] [13:00] (call ends)
